acceptance_checks: A lease held by a live process reads `held`, and the loop returns wait_runner naming it.
After that process is killed, the same lease reads `free` and the loop re-dispatches the task.
A lease file recording a different host reads `foreign_host`; the loop stays wait_runner and never re-dispatches.
A `running` task with no lease file at all is re-dispatched.
Re-dispatch is bounded by a module constant defaulting to 2, and exceeding it returns stop_blocked with a reason naming the attempt count and the free lease.
session_lease_state never leaves the lock held: two consecutive probes return the same state.
A second dispatch for a task whose lease is held fails with the collision message instead of starting a second session.
dispatch_runner_task holds the lease across the status=running write and the adapter call, and releases it on both success and failure.
.shiki/leases is declared local-only in .shiki/manifest.json and ignored by .gitignore.
tests/test_session_lease.py drives real processes and the real loop decision for every case above.
No file outside the declared locks is changed.
non_goals: Changing what a healthy session does
Judging a lease taken on another host
Tracking the lease directory in git or the mirror
Changing repair, CCA or MergeGate semantics
Touching any file outside the declared locks

findings.detail: The re-dispatch budget (dispatch_attempts) increments only on the redispatch action and is never reset when a session completes normally, so the bound is cumulative across the task's whole life rather than per dead-session episode. This is a conservative fail-safe (it can only stop sooner) and matches the plan's intent, so it is not a defect — flagging only so a future reader knows the counter is not per-episode.
findings.title: dispatch_attempts is cumulative over the task lifetime, never reset after a healthy dispatch

findings.detail: Adding `import fcntl`/`import socket` at the top of shiki_runtime hard-binds the module (and everything importing it, e.g. shiki_loop/shiki_cli/validate_shiki's module-import check) to POSIX. Shiki is already Unix-targeted (macOS/Linux) and validate_shiki_cli_module_boundaries imports shiki_runtime successfully on those platforms, so this is not a regression — noted only as a new hard platform dependency introduced at import time.
findings.title: scripts/shiki_runtime.py now imports fcntl at module top, making it Unix-only at import time

scope:
Add `scripts/shiki_session_lease.py` with two operations over `<target>/.shiki/leases/<task_id>.lock`:
  - `hold_session_lease(target, task_id)` — a context manager used by the dispatching process. It opens the lease file, takes `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)`, writes `{task_id, host, pid, started_at, attempt}` as the file's content, and holds the descriptor for the lifetime of the session. It releases on exit and on process death alike, because the kernel releases it.
  - `session_lease_state(target, task_id)` — a read-only probe returning one of `held` (a non-blocking acquire FAILED, so a holder is alive), `free` (the acquire SUCCEEDED and was immediately released, so no holder remains), `foreign_host` (the file records a host other than this one — never judged), or `absent` (no lease file). It must never leave the lease acquired.

In `scripts/shiki_runtime.py`, wrap the body of `dispatch_runner_task` from the `task["status"] = "running"` write through the adapter call in `hold_session_lease`. If the lease cannot be taken, another dispatch for the same task is already running: fail with that exact message rather than starting a second session against the same worktree.

In `scripts/shiki_loop.py`, `decide_task_action` currently returns `wait_runner` for every `running` task (line 88). It must now consult the lease: `held` or `foreign_host` keeps `wait_runner` with the reason naming which; `free` or `absent` means the session is gone. On a gone session, return a new action that resets the task to `ready` and re-dispatches, recording the attempt on the task (a `dispatch_attempts` integer). Past the bound — default 2, declared as a module constant — return `stop_blocked` with a reason that names the task, the attempt count and the fact that the lease was free, so the operator sees why it stopped rather than a generic block.

Register `.shiki/leases` in `.shiki/manifest.json` with `state_class: local-only` (already declared in the manifest's state_classes and already treated as untracked by `shiki_state_classes.is_untracked_path`) and add it to `.gitignore`.

Add `tests/test_session_lease.py` driving real processes and the real loop decision, not mocks of the lease: a lease held by a live child process reads `held` and the loop stays wait_runner; the same lease after that child is killed reads `free` and the loop re-dispatches; a lease file naming a foreign host reads `foreign_host` and the loop stays wait_runner and never re-dispatches; an absent lease on a `running` task re-dispatches; the bound is respected and the stop reason names the attempt count; `session_lease_state` leaves no lock held (probing twice in a row gives the same answer); a second dispatch for a task whose lease is held fails with the collision message. Add a case to `scripts/test_shiki_runner_claude.sh` asserting that a normal dispatch takes and releases the lease.

REPRODUCIBILITY — what this task removes, and what to change to get the same result.
  Symptom: a task sits at status `running` and the loop reports `wait_runner: implementer session is running` on every step, forever. `ps` shows no session. The only recovery is an operator running `shiki task status --status ready <id>` by hand, and the only way to know it is needed is to notice the loop has not advanced.
  Measured: reproduced three times on 2026-07-29..31 by running `shiki loop step` in the foreground, where the 10-minute command timeout killed the dispatched session mid-work. Each time the task remained `running` with zero live processes. `scripts/shiki_runtime.py` writes `running` before a synchronous adapter call and writes the terminal status only after it returns, so any death between those two writes strands the task. `grep -n 'heartbeat|pid' scripts/shiki_loop.py` returns nothing — there is no liveness signal of any kind.
  Why flock and not a pid: a recorded pid can be reused by an unrelated process after the session dies, which turns a stranded task into a permanently 'alive' one — strictly worse than today, because the operator would have positive evidence for a false conclusion. An flock is released by the kernel on process death, so a successful non-blocking acquire is exact.
  Exact change that reproduces this result: hold an exclusive flock for the session's lifetime, and make the loop's `running` branch consult it instead of trusting the status field.
  Reproducible when: killing a dispatched session and stepping the loop re-dispatches it automatically, and a live session is never disturbed.
test_command: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests && bash scripts/test_shiki_runner_claude.sh && bash scripts/test_shiki_goal_loop.sh && python3 scripts/validate_shiki.py --target .
title: Prove a runner session is alive with an OS lease and recover a dead one
